notes.front: What is a security plan, under subpart I of part 172?
notes.back: A transportation security plan that each person offering or transporting certain listed hazardous materials must develop and adhere to.
notes.explanation: Subpart I exists to address security risks in transporting hazardous materials; § 172.800(b) lists the materials that trigger it.
notes.example: Like a site’s fire plan, but aimed at theft, sabotage and misuse of the hazardous materials it ships.
notes.evidence: Each person who offers for transportation in commerce or transports in commerce one or more of the following hazardous materials must develop and adhere to a transportation security plan for hazardous materials that conforms to the requirements of this subpart.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.800(a)–(b), PDF p. 306

notes.front: What is a large bulk quantity, for security plans?
notes.back: More than 3,000 kg (6,614 pounds) of solids, or more than 3,000 litres (792 gallons) of liquids and gases, in a single packaging.
notes.explanation: The rule gives cargo tank motor vehicles, portable tanks and tank cars as examples of such a single packaging.
notes.example: Like a full road tanker of fuel, but not a 1,000-litre tote on a pallet.
notes.evidence: ‘‘large bulk quantity’’ refers to a quantity greater than 3,000 kg (6,614 pounds) for solids or 3,000 liters (792 gallons) for liquids and gases in a single packaging such as a cargo tank motor vehicle, portable tank, tank car, or other bulk container.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.800(b), PDF p. 306

notes.front: What quantity of Division 1.1, 1.2 or 1.3 material requires a security plan?
notes.back: Any quantity.
notes.explanation: These are among the few materials on the list that trigger a plan in any amount.
notes.evidence: (1) Any quantity of a Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 material.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.800(b)(1), PDF p. 306

notes.front: What quantity of Division 1.4, 1.5 or 1.6 material requires a security plan?
notes.back: A quantity that requires placarding under subpart F.
notes.explanation: The placarding rules, not a separate figure, set the trigger for these divisions.
notes.evidence: (2) A quantity of a Division 1.4, 1.5, or 1.6 material requiring placarding in accordance with subpart F of this part.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.800(b)(2), PDF p. 306

notes.front: What quantity of Division 2.1 (flammable gas) requires a security plan?
notes.back: A large bulk quantity.
notes.explanation: Only a single packaging holding more than 3,000 litres counts.
notes.evidence: (3) A large bulk quantity of Division 2.1 material.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.800(b)(3), PDF p. 306

notes.front: Which Division 2.2 material requires a security plan, and in what quantity?
notes.back: Division 2.2 material with a subsidiary hazard of 5.1, in a large bulk quantity.
notes.explanation: Other Division 2.2 gases are not on the list.
notes.evidence: (4) A large bulk quantity of Division 2.2 material with a subsidiary hazard of 5.1.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.800(b)(4), PDF p. 306

notes.front: What quantity of a material poisonous by inhalation requires a security plan?
notes.back: Any quantity.
notes.explanation: Division 6.1 material that is not poisonous by inhalation needs a large bulk quantity instead.
notes.evidence: (5) Any quantity of a material poisonous by inhalation, as defined in § 171.8 of this subchapter.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.800(b)(5), PDF p. 306

notes.front: Which Class 3 material requires a security plan, and in what quantity?
notes.back: Class 3 meeting Packing Group I or II criteria, in a large bulk quantity.
notes.explanation: Packing Group III flammable liquids are not on the list.
notes.evidence: (6) A large bulk quantity of a Class 3 material meeting the criteria for Packing Group I or II.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.800(b)(6), PDF p. 306

notes.front: What quantity of desensitized explosives requires a security plan?
notes.back: A quantity that requires placarding, when they meet the definition of Division 4.1 or Class 3 material.
notes.explanation: Like Divisions 1.4 to 1.6, the trigger is tied to placarding.
notes.evidence: (7) A quantity of desensitized explosives meeting the definition of Division 4.1 or Class 3 material requiring placarding in accordance with subpart F of this part.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.800(b)(7), PDF p. 306

notes.front: Which Division 4.2 material requires a security plan, and in what quantity?
notes.back: Division 4.2 meeting Packing Group I or II criteria, in a large bulk quantity.
notes.explanation: Class 3, Division 4.2 and Division 5.1 share the Packing Group I or II and large bulk pattern.
notes.evidence: (8) A large bulk quantity of a Division 4.2 material meeting the criteria for Packing Group I or II.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.800(b)(8), PDF p. 306

notes.front: What quantity of Division 4.3 material requires a security plan?
notes.back: A quantity that requires placarding under subpart F.
notes.explanation: Division 4.3 is in placarding Table 1, which has no weight allowance, so even a small quantity can need placards and therefore a plan.
notes.evidence: (9) A quantity of a Division 4.3 material requiring placarding in accordance with subpart F of this part.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.800(b)(9), PDF p. 306

notes.front: Which Division 5.1 materials require a security plan in a large bulk quantity?
notes.back: Packing Groups I and II; perchlorates; and ammonium nitrate, ammonium nitrate fertilizers, or ammonium nitrate emulsions, suspensions or gels.
notes.explanation: Each of these is listed only in a large bulk quantity.
notes.evidence: (10) A large bulk quantity of a Division 5.1 material in Packing Groups I and II; perchlorates; or ammonium nitrate, ammonium nitrate fertilizers, or
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.800(b)(10), PDF p. 306

notes.front: Which organic peroxide requires a security plan in any quantity?
notes.back: Organic peroxide, Type B, liquid or solid, temperature controlled.
notes.explanation: The same material is the one Division 5.2 entry in placarding Table 1.
notes.evidence: (11) Any quantity of organic peroxide, Type B, liquid or solid, temperature controlled.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.800(b)(11), PDF p. 307

notes.front: What quantity of Division 6.1 material (other than poisonous by inhalation) requires a security plan?
notes.back: A large bulk quantity.
notes.explanation: Material poisonous by inhalation is covered separately, in any quantity.
notes.evidence: (12) A large bulk quantity of Division 6.1 material (for a material poisonous by inhalation see paragraph (5) above).
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.800(b)(12), PDF p. 307

notes.front: Which biological materials require a security plan?
notes.back: A select agent or toxin regulated by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention or the U.S. Department of Agriculture.
notes.explanation: No quantity threshold is set for this item.
notes.evidence: (13) A select agent or toxin regulated by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention under 42 CFR part 73 or the U.S. Department of Agriculture under 9 CFR part 121.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.800(b)(13), PDF p. 307

notes.front: What quantity of uranium hexafluoride requires a security plan?
notes.back: A quantity that requires placarding under § 172.505(b).
notes.explanation: § 172.505(b) requires CORROSIVE and POISON placards from 454 kg gross weight.
notes.evidence: (14) A quantity of uranium hexafluoride requiring placarding under § 172.505(b).
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.800(b)(14), PDF p. 307

notes.front: Which radioactive materials require a security plan under § 172.800(b)(15)?
notes.back: Category 1 and 2 materials under the International Atomic Energy Agency Code of Conduct and Nuclear Regulatory Commission lists, and highway route controlled quantities.
notes.explanation: Item (15) combines several radioactive categories in one entry.
notes.evidence: International Atomic Energy Agency Code of Conduct (IBR, see § 171.7) Category 1 and 2 materials, Nuclear Regulatory Commission, Category 1 and Category 2 radioactive materials
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.800(b)(15), PDF p. 307

notes.front: Which Class 8 material requires a security plan, and in what quantity?
notes.back: Class 8 meeting Packing Group I criteria, in a large bulk quantity.
notes.explanation: Class 8 is the one item limited to Packing Group I alone.
notes.evidence: (16) A large bulk quantity of Class 8 material meeting the criteria for Packing Group I.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.800(b)(16), PDF p. 307

notes.front: A cargo tank carries 9,000 litres of a Class 3 Packing Group II liquid. Does the carrier need a security plan?
notes.back: D: yes; it is a large bulk quantity of Class 3 Packing Group II.
notes.choices:
A) No, Class 3 is never listed
B) No, only Packing Group I is listed
C) Only if it also carries explosives
D) Yes, it is a large bulk quantity of Class 3 Packing Group II
notes.choicesExplained: A: § 172.800(b)(6) lists Class 3 in a large bulk quantity. B: Packing Group I or II qualifies for Class 3; Packing Group I alone is the Class 8 item. C: the Class 3 item stands on its own.
notes.explanation: 9,000 litres in one packaging is well over the 3,000 litre threshold, and Packing Group II qualifies.
notes.evidence: (6) A large bulk quantity of a Class 3 material meeting the criteria for Packing Group I or II.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.800(b)(6), PDF p. 306

notes.front: A truck carries eight 1,000-litre totes of a Class 3 Packing Group II liquid, 8,000 litres in all. Is that a large bulk quantity?
notes.back: B: no; large bulk quantity is measured in a single packaging, and each tote holds only 1,000 litres.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, because the total is over 3,000 litres
B) No, because each single packaging holds only 1,000 litres
C) Yes, because totes are bulk packagings
D) No, because liquids are measured in kilograms
notes.choicesExplained: A: the rule measures the quantity in a single packaging, not the load. C: being bulk is not enough; the single packaging must exceed 3,000 litres. D: liquids and gases are measured in litres; kilograms are for solids.
notes.explanation: The threshold is per packaging, so separate containers are not added together.
notes.evidence: a quantity greater than 3,000 kg (6,614 pounds) for solids or 3,000 liters (792 gallons) for liquids and gases in a single packaging
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.800(b), PDF p. 306

notes.front: A tank truck carries 6,000 litres of a Class 8 Packing Group II liquid, and nothing else. Does § 172.800(b) require a security plan?
notes.back: A: no; Class 8 is listed only for Packing Group I in a large bulk quantity.
notes.choices:
A) No, Class 8 is listed only for Packing Group I
B) Yes, any large bulk quantity requires a plan
C) Yes, all Class 8 requires a plan
D) Only if the tank is placarded
notes.choicesExplained: B: large bulk quantity triggers a plan only for the listed materials. C: only Packing Group I Class 8, in large bulk, is listed. D: placarding is not the trigger for Class 8.
notes.explanation: Large bulk alone does not trigger a plan; the material must also match a listed item.
notes.evidence: (16) A large bulk quantity of Class 8 material meeting the criteria for Packing Group I.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.800(b)(16), PDF p. 307

notes.front: Since 3 September 2026, below what gross receipts is a farmer excepted from the security plan requirements?
notes.back: Less than $825,000 in 2025 dollars annually from the sale of agricultural commodities or products.
notes.explanation: The threshold is expressed in 2025 dollars, as set by the 2026 amendment.
notes.evidence: Transportation activities of a farmer, who generates less than $825,000 in 2025 dollars annually in gross receipts from the sale of agricultural commodities or products, are not subject to this subpart
notes.source: Hazardous Materials: Reduce Training Burdens for America’s Farmers, 91 FR 49329 (final rule, 4 August 2026), § 172.800(c) as amended by 91 FR 49329, PDF p. 4

notes.front: Under § 172.800(c), what three conditions must a qualifying farmer’s transportation activities meet?
notes.back: By highway or rail; in direct support of the farming operations; and within a 150-mile radius of those operations.
notes.explanation: All three must hold, together with the gross receipts limit, for the exception to apply.
notes.evidence: (1) Conducted by highway or rail; (2) In direct support of their farming operations; and (3) Conducted within a 150-mile radius of those operations.
notes.source: Hazardous Materials: Reduce Training Burdens for America’s Farmers, 91 FR 49329 (final rule, 4 August 2026), § 172.800(c) as amended by 91 FR 49329, PDF p. 4

notes.front: Are farmers exempt from the security plan also exempt from in-depth security training?
notes.back: Yes. Farmers exempt under § 172.800(c) are also exempt from the in-depth security training in § 172.704(a)(5).
notes.explanation: This follows from qualifying for the amended § 172.800(c) exception.
notes.evidence: Farmers who are exempt from the security plan requirements in 49 CFR 172.800(c) are also exempt from the in-depth security training requirements for hazardous materials employees in 49 CFR 172.704(a)(5).
notes.source: Hazardous Materials: Reduce Training Burdens for America’s Farmers, 91 FR 49329 (final rule, 4 August 2026), 91 FR 49329, “What action is PHMSA taking in this final rule?”, PDF p. 1

notes.front: A farm with $700,000 a year in crop sales trucks its own fertilizer 200 miles to a second field it farms. Is it excepted from the security plan requirement?
notes.back: B: no; the activity is outside the 150-mile radius, so the exception does not apply.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, its receipts are under $825,000
B) No, the trip is outside the 150-mile radius
C) Yes, because it is its own fertilizer
D) No, farms are never excepted
notes.choicesExplained: A: the receipts limit is only one condition; the 150-mile radius must also be met. C: direct support is also only one condition. D: § 172.800(c) does except qualifying farmers.
notes.explanation: The receipts are under the $825,000 threshold, but every condition must be met, including the 150-mile radius.
notes.evidence: Conducted within a 150-mile radius of those operations.
notes.source: Hazardous Materials: Reduce Training Burdens for America’s Farmers, 91 FR 49329 (final rule, 4 August 2026), § 172.800(c) as amended by 91 FR 49329, PDF p. 4

notes.front: What assessment must a security plan include?
notes.back: An assessment of transportation security risks, including site-specific risks at facilities where the materials are prepared, stored or unloaded, and measures to address them.
notes.explanation: The assessment covers the facilities as well as the shipments themselves.
notes.evidence: The security plan must include an assessment of transportation security risks for shipments of the hazardous materials listed in § 172.800, including site-specific or location-specific risks associated with facilities
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.802(a), PDF p. 307

notes.front: A company writes a security plan that covers its trucks on the road but says nothing about the yard where drums wait for collection. What is missing?
notes.back: A: site-specific risks at facilities where the materials are prepared, stored or unloaded incidental to movement.
notes.choices:
A) Site-specific risks at the facilities where materials are prepared, stored or unloaded
B) Nothing; plans cover only vehicles
C) A list of drivers’ home addresses
D) A copy of each shipping paper
notes.choicesExplained: B: § 172.802(a) expressly includes facility risks. C: the rule does not ask for this. D: the plan’s contents are the risk assessment and security measures, not shipping papers.
notes.explanation: The risk assessment must cover those facilities as well as shipments en route.
notes.evidence: site-specific or location-specific risks associated with facilities at which the hazardous materials listed in § 172.800 are prepared for transportation, stored, or unloaded incidental to movement
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.802(a), PDF p. 307

notes.front: What does the personnel security element of a security plan require?
notes.back: Measures to confirm information given by job applicants hired for positions involving access to and handling of the covered materials.
notes.explanation: The confirmation system must be consistent with Federal and State employment and privacy law.
notes.evidence: Personnel security. Measures to confirm information provided by job applicants hired for positions that involve access to and handling of the hazardous materials covered by the security plan. Such confirmation system must be consistent with applicable Federal and State laws and requirements concerning employment practices and individual privacy.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.802(a)(1), PDF p. 307

notes.front: What does the unauthorised access element of a security plan require?
notes.back: Measures to address the assessed risk that unauthorised persons may gain access to the covered materials or to conveyances being prepared to carry them.
notes.explanation: It covers vehicles being prepared for the materials, not just the materials themselves.
notes.evidence: Unauthorized access. Measures to address the assessed risk that unauthorized persons may gain access to the hazardous materials covered by the security plan or transport conveyances being prepared for transportation
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.802(a)(2), PDF p. 307

notes.front: What does the en route security element of a security plan cover?
notes.back: The assessed security risks of shipments of the covered materials from origin to destination, including shipments stored incidental to movement.
notes.explanation: Storage during the journey counts as part of en route security.
notes.evidence: En route security. Measures to address the assessed security risks of shipments of hazardous materials covered by the security plan en route from origin to destination, including shipments stored incidental to movement.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.802(a)(3), PDF p. 307

notes.front: A company fits a locked gate and badge-controlled entry at its yard, so outsiders cannot reach its explosives or the trailers being loaded with them. Which security plan element is this?
notes.back: B: unauthorised access.
notes.choices:
A) Personnel security
B) Unauthorised access
C) Training plan
D) En route security
notes.choicesExplained: A: personnel security is about confirming job applicants’ information. C: the training plan concerns training hazmat employees. D: en route security covers shipments from origin to destination, not access at the yard.
notes.explanation: Keeping unauthorised persons away from the materials or the conveyances being prepared is the unauthorised access element.
notes.evidence: Measures to address the assessed risk that unauthorized persons may gain access to the hazardous materials covered by the security plan
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.802(a)(2), PDF p. 307

notes.front: How must a security plan identify the person responsible for it?
notes.back: By job title, naming the senior management official responsible for overall development and implementation of the plan.
notes.explanation: The plan names a post, not a person.
notes.evidence: Identification by job title of the senior management official responsible for overall development and implementation of the security plan;
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.802(b)(1), PDF p. 307

notes.front: Besides the responsible official, what two further items must § 172.802(b) plans contain?
notes.back: Security duties for each responsible position or department, with how employees are told to implement elements; and a plan for training hazmat employees.
notes.explanation: The training plan must follow § 172.704(a)(4) and (a)(5): security awareness and in-depth security training.
notes.evidence: (2) Security duties for each position or department that is responsible for implementing the plan or a portion of the plan and the process of notifying employees when specific elements of the security plan must be implemented; and (3) A plan for training hazmat employees in accordance with § 172.704 (a)(4) and (a)(5) of this part.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.802(b)(2)–(3), PDF p. 307

notes.front: A draft security plan names “Jo, our safety lead” as responsible for it. What does § 172.802(b)(1) require instead?
notes.back: A: identification by job title of the senior management official responsible for developing and implementing the plan.
notes.choices:
A) The senior management official, identified by job title
B) Every employee by name
C) The carrier’s driver
D) No named person is needed
notes.choicesExplained: B: duties are set by position or department, not a list of every name. C: the official is a senior manager responsible for the plan. D: § 172.802(b)(1) requires the official to be identified.
notes.explanation: The rule asks for the senior management official, identified by job title.
notes.evidence: Identification by job title of the senior management official responsible for overall development and implementation of the security plan;
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.802(b)(1), PDF p. 307

notes.front: In what form must a security plan be kept, and for how long?
notes.back: In writing, retained for as long as it remains in effect, including its risk assessment.
notes.explanation: The risk assessment is kept with it, as part of the written plan.
notes.evidence: The security plan, including the transportation security risk assessment developed in accordance with paragraph (a) of this section, must be in writing and must be retained for as long as it remains in effect.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.802(c), PDF p. 307

notes.front: How often must a security plan be reviewed?
notes.back: At least annually, and revised or updated as needed to reflect changing circumstances.
notes.explanation: Review is yearly; revision follows whenever circumstances change.
notes.evidence: The security plan must be reviewed at least annually and revised and/or updated as necessary to reflect changing circumstances.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.802(c), PDF p. 307

notes.front: A company’s security plan was last reviewed 20 months ago, and nothing has changed since. Is it compliant?
notes.back: B: no; the plan must be reviewed at least annually, whether or not circumstances have changed.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, because nothing has changed
B) No, it must be reviewed at least annually
C) Yes, plans are reviewed every three years
D) Yes, if the senior official still holds the post
notes.choicesExplained: A: the review is due every year even if no revision results. C: three years is the recurrent training cycle, not the plan review. D: who holds the post does not affect the review duty.
notes.explanation: Revision depends on changing circumstances, but the annual review does not.
notes.evidence: must be reviewed at least annually
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.802(c), PDF p. 307

notes.front: To whom must a security plan be made available on request?
notes.back: An authorised official of the Department of Transportation or the Department of Homeland Security, at a reasonable time and location.
notes.explanation: The copy, or an electronic file, must be accessible at or through the principal place of business.
notes.evidence: must maintain a copy of the security plan (or an electronic file thereof) that is accessible at, or through, its principal place of business and must make the security plan available upon request, at a reasonable time and location, to an authorized official of the Department of Transportation or the Department of Homeland Security.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.802(d), PDF p. 308

notes.front: May a security plan written for another Federal agency or an industry body satisfy subpart I?
notes.back: Yes, if it addresses the requirements specified in subpart I.
notes.explanation: The rule allows this to avoid unnecessary duplication of security requirements.
notes.evidence: To avoid unnecessary duplication of security requirements, security plans that conform to regulations, standards, protocols, or guidelines issued by other Federal agencies, international organizations, or industry organizations may be used to satisfy the requirements in this subpart
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.804, PDF p. 308
